FrMS88-de6363-d1e111.summary: Poses the eighteenth question: whether by divine power there can be intuitive knowledge of a non-existent. Against: Genesis, 'God saw all that he had made'.
claims: Genesis suggests God saw things as made, i.e. existing.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e122.summary: Contrary: Ambrose says angels knew things before they existed. Two contradictory opinions exist; the first affirms the question, arguing first: what God can do through a secondary cause he can do by himself, and he causes intuitive knowledge through the object as secondary cause, so he can without the object.
claims: Reported view: God can cause intuitive knowledge without the object, since he can do without secondary causes what he does through them.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e135.summary: Second argument: on Meyronnes' own view intuitive and abstractive agree in terminating and differ in moving, and God can supply every moving role.
claims: Reported argument: God can supply the object's moving role.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e146.summary: Third argument: God can separate any disparate absolutes, and the act is an absolute distinct from the object.
claims: Reported argument: the act, as an absolute, can be separated from its object.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e154.summary: Fourth argument: the act can be separated from the intellect, so from the object, since the act has more and more intimate relations to the intellect (as dependent effect and inherent accident) than to the object. They conclude that God can cause intuitive knowledge without the object, keeping every condition of intuition.
claims: Reported argument: if the act is separable from the intellect it is separable from the object.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e180.summary: Others of this view say the quality would remain but not its relation to the object.
claims: Reported variant: the quality remains without its relation to the object.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e185.summary: Others say the absolute would remain but be neither intuitive knowledge, for lack of an object, nor abstractive, since not through a representative.
claims: Reported variant: the act would be neither intuitive nor abstractive.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e194.summary: Others say knowledge would remain, but abstractive, since had through another.
claims: Reported variant: the act would become abstractive.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e199.summary: Meyronnes holds none of these and argues first against the claim that God can cause knowledge without the object under every condition it has when the object causes it.
claims: God cannot cause, without the object, knowledge identical in every condition to object-caused knowledge.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e208.summary: Argues from Augustine: the divine intellect produces or speaks nothing ad extra, so cannot speak a word in us; but knowledge caused by the object is a word.
claims: God speaks no word ad extra; object-caused knowledge is a word.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e216.summary: Similarly for spiration: God spirates nothing ad extra, so cannot produce a spirated love in our soul; though God can cause every absolute, not under every condition, at least not under a respect; he can produce an act of love in us but not, with all his powers, an act of spirating.
claims: God can cause every absolute but not under every respect or condition.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e232.summary: Against the second variant: the act of understanding and knowledge are two; the act is a quality and not a pure perfection, while knowledge expresses a respect to the object and is a pure perfection; if only the quality remained, it would not be knowledge and nothing would be understood.
claims: The act of understanding is a quality; knowledge is a respect to the object and a pure perfection.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e243.summary: Against the third variant: variation does not occur precisely through the respect, so removing the respect would not vary the act.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e250.summary: Against the fourth variant: the rule 'whatever God can do...' would then have four terms, since the minor would speak of intuitive knowledge with the object and the conclusion of abstractive. Turns to answer the arguments for the first opinion.
claims: The variant commits a fallacy of four terms.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e259.summary: Reply to the first argument: God can act without the object as cause, but not without it as terminus — as a ray made by God would be a ray but would lack the relation of passive generation from the sun, so the act would lack the relation of being produced by the object.
claims: God can replace the object as cause but not as terminus.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e277.summary: Reply to the second: intuitive and abstractive differ in their terminating notion, since intuitive concerns existence while abstractive terminates at the quiddity as abstracted from existence.
claims: Intuitive and abstractive cognition differ in how they terminate: existence vs. quiddity.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e287.summary: Reply to the third: God can separate disparate absolutes, but the act is not disparate with respect to its object.
claims: The act of knowledge is not disparate from its object.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e296.summary: Reply to the fourth: knowledge has two respects, as accident to subject and as knowledge to object, and the second is more essential. Then presents the contrary opinion: intuitive knowledge cannot exist without the real presence of its object, since one cannot see where nothing is seen. Argument: intuitive knowledge is of the singular; knowledge terminating at an object actuated with ultimate actuality bears on it as existing; singularity is ultimate actuality.
claims: The relation of knowledge to its object is more essential than its relation to its subject.
Intuitive cognition of the singular, as ultimate actuality, requires an existing object.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e327.summary: Second argument: nothing accidental can belong to something existing only in potency, but intuition knows what belongs to a thing per accidens. Proof: a thing's potential being is necessary and has nothing from another; and since existence is essentially prior to any accident in a subject, an accident cannot inhere unless existence does.
claims: Nothing accidental belongs to a thing in potential being.
Existence is essentially prior to accidents.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e358.summary: Third argument, returning to the same: nothing can belong contingently to a being in potency, and intuitive cognition as such is contingent, so it cannot regard a being in potency.
claims: Intuitive cognition, being contingent, cannot regard a merely potential being.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e369.summary: Fourth argument: in essentially ordered things the posterior cannot be without the prior; existence is prior to accidental features, so these cannot be known to inhere unless the thing actually exists.
claims: Accidents cannot be known to inhere in a non-existent.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e380.summary: Announces four conclusions drawn from what has been said.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e384.summary: First conclusion: intuitive cognition is caused by the object.
claims: Intuitive cognition is caused by its object.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e389.summary: Second conclusion: it terminates at the object.
claims: Intuitive cognition terminates at its object.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e392.summary: Third conclusion: God can supply the object's role as mover.
claims: God can supply the object as moving cause.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e397.summary: Fourth conclusion: God cannot supply the object's role as terminus. Then raises two difficulties, the first: when things are essentially ordered and really distinct God can make one without the other, and the relation of knowledge differs really from the act and is essentially posterior.
claims: God cannot supply the object as terminus.
Objection: the knowledge-relation is really distinct from the act and so separable.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e410.summary: Second difficulty: whatever depends on something depends in some genus of cause; the act depends on the object; in which genus?
claims: Objection: the act's dependence on the object must be a kind of causality.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e419.summary: Reply to the first: things that cannot be separated are really the same; knowledge and its relation to the object are really the same, though distinguished in some way.
claims: Knowledge and its relation to the object are really identical though distinct in some way.

FrMS88-de6363-d1e429.summary: Reply to the second: dependence that means presupposition need not reduce to a genus of cause — action presupposes the approach of agent to patient, which is not a cause, and some hold the will's act presupposes the intellect's without being caused by it; so with the act and its object.
claims: Dependence as presupposition is not necessarily causal.

FrMS88-de6363.summary: The eighteenth question of the prologue asks whether, by divine power, there can be intuitive knowledge of a non-existent. Meyronnes sets out two contradictory opinions. The first affirms it: God can do without a secondary cause what he does through it; he can supply every moving role of the object; he can separate disparate absolutes such as the act and its object; and since he can separate the act from the intellect, with which it has more intimate relations, he can separate it from the object. Variants hold that the quality remains without its relation to the object, or remains as neither intuitive nor abstractive knowledge, or remains as abstractive. Meyronnes rejects all of these: God cannot produce externally a 'word' or a spirated love in us under every condition, since he produces and spirates nothing ad extra; knowledge, unlike the mere quality of the act, is a respect to the object and a pure perfection; and the knowledge-relation is more essential to the act than its relation to the subject. God can supply the object as cause but not as terminus, as a ray made directly by God would lack passive generation from the sun. The contrary opinion, that intuitive knowledge requires the object's real presence, argues that intuition of the singular, which is ultimate actuality, requires existence, and that a thing in potency can have nothing accidental or contingent, whereas intuition knows accidents, which presuppose existence. He concludes: intuitive cognition is caused by and terminates at its object; God can supply the object as mover but not as terminus. Knowledge and its relation to the object are really the same though distinct in some way, and the act's dependence on the object is a presupposition, not a kind of causation.
claims: Intuitive cognition of a non-existent cannot occur even by divine power, since the object is required as terminus.
God can supply the object's role as moving cause but not as terminating object.
Knowledge, as opposed to the mere quality of the act, is a respect to the object and a pure perfection.
Intuitive cognition of the singular requires the existence of its object.
Nothing accidental belongs to a thing in merely potential being.
Knowledge and its relation to the object are really identical though distinct in some way.
The act's dependence on its object is a presupposition, not a kind of causality.
